problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 1
problems.lesson_text: Educational systems often rely on the intuitive metaphor of the mind as a **"spatial storage cabinet"** or hard drive
problems.source_text: A metaphor people commonly use to think about encoding and retrieving memories is that of spatial storage and search (Roediger, 1980). ... This mental file cabinet view of the mind and memory is compelling
problems.reason: The quoted phrase blends two different source phrases ('spatial storage and search' and 'mental file cabinet') into wording the source never uses.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Far transfer, cognitive set-shifting, and novel problem solving (Chi et al., 1994; Bargh & Schul, 1980).
problems.source_text: The students who self-explained showed larger gains in comprehension of concepts in the text. ... Students who prepared to teach others performed better on the assessment than students who simply read and studied the material.
problems.reason: The source credits these studies with gains in comprehension and test performance; far transfer and cognitive set-shifting are outcomes it never mentions.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 3
problems.lesson_text: In physics instruction, prompting students to explain why velocity changes when radius contracts significantly outperforms diagram memorization (McDaniel & Donnelly, 1996).
problems.source_text: those who engaged in elaborative interrogation outperformed learners who produced labeled diagrams of the concepts in each brief text.
problems.reason: In the source, the comparison group produced labeled diagrams; it did not memorize diagrams, so the lesson misstates the study.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Novices who articulate the rationale of worked examples generate deeper conceptual understanding of complex systems, such as the human circulatory system (Chi et al., 1994).
problems.source_text: Eighth-grade students learned about the circulatory system by reading an expository text. While one group just read the text, a second group of students produced explanations for each sentence in the text.
problems.reason: Chi et al. (1994) had students explain each sentence of a text they read, not the reasoning behind worked examples.

problems.reason: Summary Street gives feedback on summaries that students write; it does not summarize for them.

problems.lesson_text: This buffers self-integrity and shields working memory from stereotype threat (Cohen et al., 2006).

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 1
problems.lesson_text: **Retention does not guarantee transfer**: As Koedinger et al. (2013) demonstrated, pedagogical strategies optimized purely for memory retention produce different cognitive outcomes than those structured for flexible, inferential transfer.
problems.source_text: not about the source
problems.reason: This point sits under 'Because recall is reconstructive:', yet nothing explains how reconstructive recall leads to the retention-versus-transfer split, so the step does not follow.

problems.location: Concept 2: Cognitive Strategies for Knowledge Retention Versus Generative Understanding / block 1
problems.lesson_text: it is a **reconstructive process** where individuals use environmental retrieval cues, current cognitive states, and prior knowledge to rebuild representations anew
problems.source_text: when people were asked in a 1995 study to listen to short lists of related words, such as bed, rest, tired, awake, dream, and snooze, and later recall as many of the words as they could, they were highly likely to recall related words that were not on the list, such as sleep
problems.reason: Reconstructive memory and reconsolidation are explained only in abstract terms, even though the source offers simple concrete cases such as the word-list and burglar/home-buyer studies.

problems.location: Concept 3: Sociocultural Goal Structures, Identity Threat, and Asset-Based Instruction / block 3

problems.source_text: In the case of women and math, for instance, women perform more poorly on the math test than would be expected given their actual ability
problems.reason: Stereotype threat is defined and explained through brain regions only, with no concrete case of it happening to a learner.
